desk.name: Acid-Base Reactions
desk.description: Select any 2 chemicals to explore acid-base chemistry — neutralizations, gas evolution, precipitates, fumes, and indicator colour changes.

reactions.name: Strong Acid + Strong Base Neutralisation

output.observation: No visible colour change. Solution becomes warm — the reaction is exothermic. Use a thermometer to observe temperature rise.

reactions.educational_note: Classic neutralization: acid + base -> salt + water. pH changes from acidic to 7 at the endpoint.

reactions.name: Two Strong Acids Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Both are strong acids and cannot react with each other.

reactions.educational_note: Acids do not react with other acids. They both release H+ ions — there is no driving force for a reaction.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids — they cannot neutralise each other.

reactions.educational_note: Mixing two acids just gives a more acidic mixture. No neutralization can occur without a base.

reactions.name: HCl + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Vigorous fizzing and bubbling. Colourless, odourless CO2 gas is produced.

reactions.educational_note: Acids react with carbonates to produce CO2 gas. Test the gas with limewater — it turns milky white, confirming CO2.

reactions.name: HCl + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: Rapid fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Faster reaction than with Na2CO3.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonates react with acids like carbonates but need only one H+ ion. Same CO2 limewater test applies.

reactions.name: HCl + Calcium Hydroxide Neutralisation

output.observation: Cloudy limewater turns clear as it is neutralised. Solution warms slightly.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater (Ca(OH)2) is a weak base. It takes twice the moles of HCl to neutralise it.

reactions.name: HCl + Ammonia -> White Fumes!

output.odor: sharp pungent — ammonia and acid combined
output.observation: Dense white fumes/smoke instantly appear where the two vapours meet in air. Very dramatic and visible!

reactions.educational_note: This reaction happens in the gas phase — no liquid mixing needed! It is used as a lab test to identify HCl and NH3 gas.

reactions.name: HCl + Phenolphthalein Indicator

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays completely colourless — confirming the solution is acidic.

reactions.educational_note: Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.2. No colour = acid or neutral.

reactions.name: HCl + Universal Indicator

output.observation: Solution turns bright RED — very strong acid at pH 1.

reactions.educational_note: Universal indicator shows exact pH by colour: red (pH 1) to violet (pH 14).

reactions.name: HCl + Litmus Indicator

output.observation: Litmus turns from purple to bright red — confirming an acid.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus is the simplest acid-base indicator. Red = acid, Blue = base.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids only react with bases, metals, or carbonates — not with each other.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + NaOH Neutralisation (Diprotic)

output.observation: Solution becomes very hot — highly exothermic. No gas or precipitate. Temperature spikes noticeably.

reactions.educational_note: H2SO4 is diprotic — needs TWICE the moles of NaOH to neutralise compared to HCl. Key for titration calculations.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + NaOH Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild heat released. Faint soapy odour from sodium acetate. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acid + strong base gives a basic salt. The endpoint pH is above 7 because sodium acetate is slightly alkaline.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both chemicals are basic.

reactions.educational_note: Bases only react with acids — not with other bases.

reactions.name: NaOH + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: No visible change. Bicarbonate is converted to carbonate by the strong base.

reactions.educational_note: A strong base converts bicarbonate to carbonate. Useful concept in buffer chemistry.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: Bases require an acid to react. Two bases simply mix without reacting.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Ammonia smell from NH3 solution. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: No acid-base reaction possible between two bases.

reactions.name: NaOH + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Solution instantly turns bright pink/magenta — confirming a strongly basic environment.

reactions.educational_note: Phenolphthalein turns pink above pH 8.2. The stronger the base, the more vivid the pink.

reactions.name: NaOH + Universal Indicator -> Violet

output.observation: Solution turns deep violet/purple — very strong base at pH 14.

reactions.educational_note: Violet = pH 12-14 on universal indicator scale = strong alkali.

reactions.name: NaOH + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns from purple to blue — confirming a base/alkali.

reactions.educational_note: Blue litmus = base. The most fundamental acid-base test.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + NaOH Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild heat released. Citrus smell fades as the acid is neutralised.

reactions.educational_note: Citric acid is triprotic — needs 3 moles of NaOH to fully neutralise 1 mole of citric acid.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids cannot react with each other in a neutralization.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Very vigorous fizzing with CO2 gas. Solution also warms due to the strong acid.

reactions.educational_note: Strong acid + carbonate reacts more vigorously than weak acid + carbonate.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Sodium Bicarbonate

output.observation: Rapid and vigorous bubbling. CO2 produced quickly. Solution warms slightly.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonate reacts with H2SO4 releasing twice the CO2 per mole.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White milky precipitate of calcium sulfate forms immediately. Solution turns cloudy white. Heat also released.

reactions.educational_note: CaSO4 is insoluble in water — precipitates as a white solid. This is how gypsum is made industrially.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Ammonia Neutralisation

output.observation: Mild white mist near the surface. Ammonia smell disappears as it reacts. Solution warms. Produces ammonium sulfate (a fertiliser).

reactions.educational_note: Ammonium sulfate is a widely used fertiliser — industrially produced by exactly this reaction.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays completely colourless — confirming an acidic environment.

reactions.educational_note: Colourless result = pH below 8.2 = acidic or neutral.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Universal Indicator -> Red

output.observation: Solution turns deep red — pH 1, strongly acidic.

reactions.educational_note: Both HCl and H2SO4 show the same red at equimolar concentrations — universal indicator cannot tell them apart.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming an acidic solution.

reactions.educational_note: All acids turn litmus red. Litmus confirms acidity but not acid strength.

reactions.name: Two Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are acids.

reactions.educational_note: Acids do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Moderate fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Vinegar smell present. Less vigorous than with strong acids.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acids react with carbonates more slowly than strong acids. CO2 limewater test still works.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Baking Soda — Classic Volcano!

output.observation: Vigorous foam and fizzing — the classic volcano reaction! Large bubbles and overflow if the container is small.

reactions.educational_note: The most famous safe acid-base reaction! Used in school volcanoes and science fairs worldwide.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Calcium Hydroxide

output.observation: Cloudy limewater becomes clear as it is neutralised. Mild heat released. Vinegar smell fades.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium acetate (product) is soluble — no precipitate forms. Solution clears as neutralisation occurs.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Ammonia

output.odor: mixed vinegar and ammonia, both fade
output.observation: Both vinegar and ammonia smells cancel out as neutralisation occurs. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Weak acid + weak base = ammonium acetate. The solution is almost perfectly neutral (pH ~7). A rare balanced neutralisation.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays colourless — confirming an acidic solution even though it is a weak acid.

reactions.educational_note: Even weak acids keep phenolphthalein colourless as long as pH stays below 8.2.

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Universal Indicator -> Orange

output.observation: Solution turns orange — weak acid at pH 3. Noticeably lighter than the red of HCl or H2SO4.

reactions.educational_note: Orange (pH 3) vs Red (pH 1): universal indicator CAN distinguish weak acids from strong acids — litmus cannot!

reactions.name: Acetic Acid + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming the solution is acidic. Vinegar smell present.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus turns red for ALL acids, weak or strong. It cannot distinguish between them.

reactions.name: Two Weak Acids Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are weak acids. Smells like salad dressing!

reactions.educational_note: Even two different acids do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Two Base Salts Mixed

output.observation: No visible reaction. Both chemicals are basic sodium salts.

reactions.educational_note: Both are alkaline sodium salts and do not react with each other.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White milky precipitate of calcium carbonate (chalk) forms instantly. Solution turns cloudy white and settles over time.

reactions.educational_note: Double displacement reaction. CaCO3 (limestone/chalk) is insoluble and precipitates. NaOH stays in solution.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are basic.

reactions.educational_note: Bases cannot react in a neutralization without an acid present.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Turns pink — confirming that sodium carbonate solution is basic (alkaline).

reactions.educational_note: Na2CO3 is a base salt — its solution is alkaline due to hydrolysis. Phenolphthalein confirms this.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue — moderately strong base at pH 11.

reactions.educational_note: pH 11 = blue. Compare to NaOH (violet, pH 14) — you can see Na2CO3 is a weaker base.

reactions.name: Na2CO3 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming sodium carbonate solution is basic.

reactions.educational_note: Even base salts like Na2CO3 turn litmus blue — their solutions are alkaline.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Sodium Carbonate

output.observation: Steady fizzing with CO2 bubbles. Citrus smell present. Moderate intensity.

reactions.educational_note: Same reaction used in bath bombs and effervescent drinks. Citric acid + carbonate = CO2 fizz.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Calcium Hydroxide -> White Precipitate

output.observation: White precipitate of CaCO3 forms. Solution becomes cloudy/milky white.

reactions.educational_note: Bicarbonate reacts with Ca(OH)2 to form insoluble CaCO3 — same principle used in water softening.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are weak bases.

reactions.educational_note: Two bases will not neutralise each other.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Phenolphthalein -> Very Faint Pink
reactions.formula: NaHCO3 (pH 8.3) -> Phenolphthalein turns VERY FAINT PINK

output.observation: A barely visible faint pink — NaHCO3 is only mildly basic (pH 8.3), just above the indicator threshold of 8.2.

reactions.educational_note: Faint pink distinguishes NaHCO3 from stronger bases like NaOH (deep pink). Great for comparing base strengths.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Universal Indicator -> Teal

output.observation: Solution turns teal/blue-green — mildly basic at pH 8. Much lighter than NaOH (violet) or Na2CO3 (blue).

reactions.educational_note: NaHCO3 is the mildest base in this set — perfect for comparing base strengths visually across all 4 bases.

reactions.name: NaHCO3 + Litmus -> Faint Blue
reactions.formula: NaHCO3 (weak base) -> Litmus turns FAINT BLUE

output.observation: Litmus turns to a faint light blue — NaHCO3 is mildly basic.

reactions.educational_note: Faint blue vs deep blue of NaOH shows baking soda is a very weak base — a great visual comparison.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Baking Soda — Effervescent Tablet!

output.observation: Gentle sustained fizzing with citrus smell — exactly like an Alka-Seltzer tablet dissolving in water.

reactions.educational_note: This is the exact reaction in effervescent tablets (Alka-Seltzer, vitamin C tablets). CO2 bubbles create the fizz.

reactions.name: Two Bases Mixed

output.observation: No reaction. Both are bases.

reactions.educational_note: Two bases cannot neutralise each other.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Pink colour forms — Ca(OH)2 is basic. Slightly less vivid than NaOH as it is a weaker base.

reactions.educational_note: Ca(OH)2 is moderately strong base. Its pink is less vivid than NaOH — demonstrates base strength differences.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue — pH 12. Darker than Na2CO3 (pH 11) but lighter than NaOH (pH 14).

reactions.educational_note: Comparing Ca(OH)2, Na2CO3, and NaOH side by side shows a clear blue to violet progression.

reactions.name: Ca(OH)2 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming limewater is basic/alkaline.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater turning litmus blue is a classic school test.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Calcium Hydroxide

output.observation: Cloudy limewater becomes clear as it is neutralised. Mild heat produced. Citrus smell fades.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium citrate is the product — used as a calcium dietary supplement and food additive.

reactions.name: NH3 + Phenolphthalein -> Pink

output.observation: Turns pink — confirming NH3 solution is basic. Ammonia smell present.

reactions.educational_note: NH3 is a weak base but pH is high enough to activate phenolphthalein. Compare its shade with NaOH.

reactions.name: NH3 + Universal Indicator -> Blue

output.observation: Solution turns blue at pH 11. Same shade as Na2CO3 — both are moderate bases at similar pH.

reactions.educational_note: NH3 and Na2CO3 both show pH ~11. Universal indicator cannot distinguish them by colour alone.

reactions.name: NH3 + Litmus -> Blue

output.observation: Litmus turns blue — confirming ammonia solution is a base.

reactions.educational_note: Even a weak base like NH3 turns litmus blue. Litmus confirms alkalinity but not strength.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Ammonia Neutralisation

output.odor: mixed citrus and ammonia, both fading
output.observation: Both citrus and ammonia smells gradually fade as they neutralise each other. No gas or colour change.

reactions.educational_note: Ammonium citrate is produced — a weak acid + weak base salt. Used in food industry as an emulsifier.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No chemical reaction. Indicators are dyes — they only respond to acids or bases, not to each other.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators react with H+ or OH- ions, not with each other.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No reaction between two indicators.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators only respond to pH changes — not to other indicators.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Phenolphthalein

output.observation: Phenolphthalein stays colourless — confirming citric acid is acidic.

reactions.educational_note: All acids keep phenolphthalein colourless. This test alone confirms something is an acid.

reactions.name: Two Indicators Mixed

output.observation: No reaction between two indicators.

reactions.educational_note: Indicators need acids or bases to show their colours — not other indicators.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Universal Indicator -> Red-Orange

output.observation: Solution turns red-orange — pH 2. Stronger than acetic acid (orange) but weaker than HCl (red).

reactions.educational_note: Citric acid at pH 2 sits between strong acids (pH 1) and acetic acid (pH 3). Universal indicator shows this beautifully.

reactions.name: Citric Acid + Litmus -> Red

output.observation: Litmus turns red — confirming citric acid is an acid. Citrus smell present.

reactions.educational_note: Litmus confirms acidity of citric acid — same red as HCl and H2SO4. Cannot distinguish acid strength.

desk.name: Combustion Reactions
desk.description: Select a fuel and a supporter/test reagent to explore combustion chemistry — complete and incomplete burning, flame colours, metal combustions, limewater tests, and soot formation.

chemicals.name: Magnesium Ribbon
chemicals.hazard: burns_bright_white — never look directly at flame

chemicals.name: Methane Gas
chemicals.hazard: flammable_gas — no naked flames near cylinder

chemicals.name: Cobalt Chloride Paper
chemicals.hazard: mild — cobalt compounds are slightly toxic

reactions.name: Magnesium Burning in Oxygen — Dazzling White Flame

output.observation: Magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame. Dense white smoke of magnesium oxide fills the gas jar. A white powdery ash (MgO) is left behind.

reactions.educational_note: Magnesium undergoes complete combustion in oxygen. The product MgO is a white solid. This is also a synthesis (combination) reaction. NEVER look directly at the flame — it emits UV radiation.

reactions.name: Magnesium Ash + Limewater — No Reaction
reactions.formula: MgO + Ca(OH)2 -> no reaction (MgO is insoluble)

output.observation: Magnesium ribbon does not react with limewater at room temperature. Limewater stays clear. The two do not combust together.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a test reagent for CO2, not a combustion supporter. Metals require an ignition source and oxygen to combust — not limewater.

reactions.name: Magnesium + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Mg + CoCl2 paper -> no combustion reaction

output.observation: No combustion reaction. Cobalt chloride paper is a moisture-detection test reagent, not a fuel or oxidant. No reaction occurs.

reactions.educational_note: Cobalt chloride paper tests for water (turns pink when wet). It does not support or cause combustion.

reactions.name: Magnesium Burns with Copper(II) Oxide — Displacement

output.observation: Vigorous reaction with bright sparks and intense heat. Reddish-brown copper metal is seen in the white ash. MgO white powder also forms.

reactions.educational_note: Magnesium displaces copper from copper oxide because Mg is more reactive than Cu. This is both a combustion-type and a displacement reaction. The reddish product confirms copper metal formation.

reactions.name: Sulfur Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, Choking Fumes

output.odor: pungent choking smell — rotten eggs / matchstick
output.observation: Sulfur burns with a beautiful pale blue flame. Dense, choking white-gray fumes of SO2 fill the gas jar. The fumes smell strongly of burning matchsticks.

reactions.educational_note: Sulfur combustion produces sulfur dioxide (SO2), an acidic gas responsible for acid rain. In a fume cupboard, SO2 can be tested by its bleaching of damp litmus paper.

reactions.name: SO2 + Limewater — Turns Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white — indicating an acidic gas. Note: SO2 gives the same limewater test as CO2, so further tests are needed to distinguish them.

reactions.educational_note: SO2 makes limewater milky (just like CO2 does). Additional tests (e.g. bleaching of potassium manganate) can distinguish SO2 from CO2. Both are acidic gases.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Relevant Test

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper tests for water. Sulfur combustion produces SO2, not water — so the paper stays blue. No water is produced when sulfur burns.

reactions.educational_note: Only fuels containing hydrogen (H) produce water when burned. Sulfur contains no hydrogen, so no water forms and cobalt chloride paper does not change colour.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Copper(II) Oxide — No Direct Combustion
reactions.formula: S + CuO -> no clean combustion at room temperature

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Sulfur and copper oxide do not combust together without very high heat input. This pair is not used in a standard combustion experiment.

reactions.educational_note: Not all pairs of combustible and oxidising materials react under normal lab conditions. Activation energy and reactivity must both be sufficient.

reactions.name: Carbon (Charcoal) Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2

output.observation: Charcoal glows orange-red and burns cleanly in pure oxygen. No visible smoke. Colourless, odourless CO2 is produced. The glow intensifies in pure O2 compared to air.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of carbon gives CO2. If oxygen is limited, incomplete combustion gives CO (carbon monoxide), a colourless, odourless, and very toxic gas.

reactions.name: CO2 Test — Limewater Turns Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white — the classic positive test for carbon dioxide. The white precipitate is calcium carbonate (chalk).

reactions.educational_note: The limewater test is the standard school test for CO2. Milky = CO2 present. If excess CO2 is bubbled through, the precipitate can redissolve forming Ca(HCO3)2.

reactions.name: Carbon Combustion + Cobalt Chloride Paper — Stays Blue

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — confirming that carbon combustion produces no water. Carbon has no hydrogen, so no H2O can form.

reactions.educational_note: Only hydrogen-containing fuels produce water on combustion. Pure carbon produces only CO2 (complete) or CO (incomplete). Cobalt chloride paper stays blue = no water.

reactions.name: Carbon Reduces Copper Oxide — Reddish Copper Appears

output.observation: Black copper oxide slowly turns reddish-brown as copper metal is produced. CO2 gas is also produced (confirmed by limewater). Carbon acts as a reducing agent.

reactions.educational_note: Carbon reduces copper oxide — a key industrial concept (blast furnace). Carbon is oxidised to CO2; copper oxide is reduced to copper. This is a redox reaction.

reactions.name: Ethanol Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.odor: faint sweet alcoholic smell near base of flame
output.observation: Ethanol burns with a near-invisible pale blue flame. No smoke or soot. Water condenses on a cool surface held above the flame. CO2 can be confirmed with limewater.

reactions.educational_note: Ethanol is a clean-burning alcohol fuel. The products are CO2 and water — same as any complete hydrocarbon combustion. Its almost invisible flame is a lab safety hazard.

reactions.name: Ethanol Combustion Products — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky
reactions.formula: CO2 (from C2H5OH combustion) + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O

output.observation: Combustion products of ethanol are bubbled through limewater. It turns milky white — confirming CO2 was produced by the ethanol burning.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater confirms CO2 in ethanol combustion products. This is a key practical skill: using a delivery tube to divert combustion gases through limewater.

reactions.name: Ethanol Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink when held in the water vapour produced by burning ethanol. This confirms water (H2O) is a product of combustion.

reactions.educational_note: Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink in the presence of water. This is the standard water test. Ethanol contains hydrogen, so burning it always produces water.

reactions.name: Ethanol + Copper Oxide — No Direct Combustion at Room Temperature

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Ethanol requires ignition to combust. Copper oxide is not an ignition source — it is an oxidising solid that requires high temperatures.

reactions.educational_note: Combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and sufficient activation energy (ignition). Just mixing ethanol and CuO does not trigger a reaction without heat.

reactions.name: Candle Wax Burns in Oxygen — Yellow Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.observation: Candle wax burns with a bright yellow-orange flame in pure oxygen. No soot. Water vapour and CO2 are produced. The flame is much brighter in pure O2 than in air.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of paraffin wax produces only CO2 and H2O. The yellow colour of a candle flame in air is due to incandescent soot particles — absent in pure oxygen.

reactions.name: Candle Combustion Products — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white as candle combustion gases are bubbled through. Positive test for CO2. The white precipitate is calcium carbonate (the same as chalk).

reactions.educational_note: This is the classic school limewater test for CO2 using a burning candle. Milky white result = CO2 confirmed. Used to prove that hydrocarbons contain carbon.

reactions.name: Candle Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper
reactions.formula: C25H52 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O (water turns paper pink)

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper held above a burning candle turns from blue to pink — confirming water vapour is produced by combustion. You may also see water droplets condense.

reactions.educational_note: The candle + cobalt chloride paper test is a standard practical. Pink = water. This proves that paraffin wax contains hydrogen — since only H-containing fuels make water.

reactions.name: Candle Wax + Copper Oxide — No Room Temperature Reaction

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Candle wax is a fuel that needs a flame to ignite. Copper oxide does not act as an ignition source under these conditions.

reactions.educational_note: The fire triangle (fuel, oxygen, heat) applies here. Wax + CuO have fuel and an oxidant but no ignition source — so no combustion occurs.

reactions.name: Methane Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.odor: odorless (methane) — slight smell from odorant added in domestic supply
output.observation: Methane burns with a clean bright blue flame in pure oxygen — no soot or smoke. CO2 and water vapour are produced. This is the cleanest burning fossil fuel.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of methane (natural gas / Bunsen burner fuel): CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. The blue flame indicates complete combustion; a yellow flame indicates incomplete combustion.

reactions.name: Methane Combustion — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky

output.observation: Methane combustion gases are passed through limewater. It turns milky white — confirming CO2 was produced. The Bunsen burner itself uses this reaction.

reactions.educational_note: The limewater test works for all carbon-containing fuels. Methane from the Bunsen burner produces CO2 that turns limewater milky.

reactions.name: Methane Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns pink when held in methane combustion gases — confirming water vapour production. Methane (CH4) has 4 hydrogen atoms, all converted to water.

reactions.educational_note: Methane has 4 hydrogen atoms → 2 water molecules per CH4 burned. Cobalt chloride paper is a quick, easy water test used alongside limewater in combustion practicals.

reactions.name: Methane + Copper Oxide — Slow Reduction at High Temperature

output.observation: When methane gas is passed over heated copper oxide, the black CuO slowly turns reddish-brown as copper metal is formed. CO2 and water vapour are also produced.

reactions.educational_note: Methane reduces copper oxide at high temperatures — a redox reaction. CuO is reduced to Cu (gains electrons); CH4 is oxidised to CO2 + H2O. Used in industry to reduce metal oxides.

reactions.name: Iron Wool Burns in Oxygen — Glowing Sparks

output.observation: Iron wool glows and showers brilliant orange sparks in pure oxygen. Black-brown iron oxide ash forms. The sparks are a dramatic and memorable demonstration.

reactions.educational_note: Iron burns in pure oxygen but not in air (too slow — it only rusts). The product Fe3O4 is magnetic. This shows that combustion supports vary in how vigorously they react.

reactions.name: Iron + Limewater — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction. Iron does not react with limewater at room temperature. Limewater is a CO2 test reagent — iron combustion produces no CO2.

reactions.educational_note: Iron combustion produces iron oxide — not CO2. So limewater stays clear. This is a useful contrast: metal combustion ≠ CO2 production.

reactions.name: Iron + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Water Produced

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — iron combustion produces no water. Iron contains no hydrogen, so water cannot be a product.

reactions.educational_note: Metals produce metal oxides when burned — not CO2 or H2O. These are key differences from hydrocarbon combustion. Cobalt chloride paper = no change confirms no water.

reactions.name: Iron + Copper Oxide — Displacement (Thermite Type)

output.observation: When heated strongly, iron displaces copper from copper oxide. Reddish-brown copper is seen in the residue alongside black iron oxide.

reactions.educational_note: Iron is higher in the reactivity series than copper, so it displaces copper from CuO. This requires strong heating — not a room temperature reaction. Iron is oxidised; copper is reduced.

reactions.name: Calcium Burns in Oxygen — Red-Orange Flame

output.ash_name: Calcium Oxide (CaO) — white, reacts with water to form Ca(OH)2
output.observation: Calcium burns with a vivid brick-red / orange flame in oxygen. White calcium oxide smoke is produced. The ash (CaO) fizzes and heats up when water is added.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium burns more vigorously than iron but less vigorously than magnesium. CaO (quicklime) is industrially important — mixed with water it forms Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime / limewater).

reactions.name: Calcium Oxide Ash + Limewater — No CO2 Test Reaction
reactions.formula: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (quicklime reacts with water in limewater)

output.observation: Calcium oxide (formed from burning calcium) reacts exothermically with water in the limewater. The mixture heats up. This is not a CO2 detection — it is CaO + H2O.

reactions.educational_note: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 (limewater) is an important reaction used industrially. However, this does not test for CO2. Only CO2 turns limewater milky by forming CaCO3.

reactions.name: Calcium Combustion — Cobalt Chloride Paper Stays Blue

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — calcium combustion produces no water. Calcium (Ca) has no hydrogen, so H2O cannot be a product.

reactions.educational_note: Metal combustion products are always metal oxides — never CO2 or H2O. Cobalt chloride paper confirms no water in metal combustion. A key distinction from hydrocarbon combustion.

reactions.name: Calcium + Copper Oxide — Calcium Displaces Copper

output.observation: Vigorous exothermic reaction with sparks and heat. Reddish-brown copper and white CaO are formed. Calcium is more reactive than copper and displaces it from its oxide.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium is high in the reactivity series (above copper), so it easily reduces CuO. This demonstrates the reactivity series through a combustion-type displacement.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Limewater — No Reaction

output.observation: Oxygen gas bubbled through limewater causes no change. Limewater only turns milky with CO2 or SO2 — not with O2.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a selective reagent — it tests for acidic gases like CO2 and SO2, not for oxygen. Oxygen is neutral and does not react with Ca(OH)2.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: O2 + CoCl2 paper -> no reaction (no water present)

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — pure oxygen gas contains no water, so no colour change. Oxygen itself is an oxidant, not a source of water.

reactions.educational_note: Cobalt chloride paper only responds to water (H2O). Pure dry oxygen gas doesn't contain H2O, so the paper stays blue. The test is simple: pink = water, blue = dry.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Copper Oxide — No Further Reaction
reactions.formula: O2 + CuO -> no reaction (CuO is already fully oxidised)

output.observation: No reaction. Copper oxide (CuO) is already fully oxidised — copper is in its +2 state and cannot be oxidised further by oxygen under normal conditions.

reactions.educational_note: CuO is a stable, fully oxidised compound. Oxygen cannot react further with it. This is why CuO is used as an oxidant in reduction reactions — it easily gives up its oxygen to fuels.

reactions.name: Limewater + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Ca(OH)2 (aq) + CoCl2 paper -> no chemical reaction

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns pink — but only because limewater is an aqueous solution (it contains water). This is not a combustion reaction; it is just moisture detection.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a solution, so it contains water. Cobalt chloride paper detects that water. Important: this does not confirm combustion products — it just shows the reagent itself is wet.

reactions.name: Limewater + Copper Oxide — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Ca(OH)2 + CuO -> no reaction at room temperature

output.observation: No significant reaction at room temperature. Limewater and copper oxide are both reagents/products of combustion reactions — they do not react with each other under these conditions.

reactions.educational_note: Both limewater and copper oxide serve as reagents in combustion experiments but don't react with each other at room temperature.

reactions.name: Cobalt Chloride Paper + Copper Oxide — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction. Both are solid reagents used in combustion experiments. They do not react with each other in any chemically meaningful way.

reactions.educational_note: Test reagents (cobalt chloride paper, limewater) are used to detect combustion products — they don't react with each other or with oxidants like CuO.

reactions.name: Iron + Sulfur → Iron(II) Sulfide

output.magnetic_note: Iron powder is magnetic before reaction; FeS product is NON-magnetic
output.observation: When the grey iron + yellow sulfur mixture is heated, a glowing red front spreads through the tube — the reaction is exothermic and self-sustaining once started. The yellow sulfur colour disappears. A new black solid, iron(II) sulfide (FeS), is formed. Unlike the iron powder mixture, the black product is NOT attracted to a magnet — proving a new compound was made, not just a mixture.

reactions.educational_note: Classic synthesis: two elements → one compound (A + B → AB). The magnet test is the key proof: iron filings are magnetic; FeS is not. This demonstrates how a compound has completely different properties from the elements that formed it. Fe + S → FeS (iron(II) sulfide, also called ferrous sulfide).

reactions.name: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium Oxide

output.observation: Magnesium burns with a blindingly bright white flame. Dense white smoke rises. A white powdery ash of magnesium oxide (MgO) remains. The product has completely different properties — MgO is a white ionic solid and a basic oxide, very different from shiny metallic magnesium or colourless oxygen gas.

reactions.educational_note: Metal + oxygen → metal oxide (basic oxide). MgO is an ionic compound with a high melting point (2852°C), very different from the metallic Mg it came from. This synthesis is also an oxidation reaction. MgO dissolves slightly in water to form Mg(OH)2, a mild base.

reactions.name: Hydrogen + Oxygen → Water

output.observation: Hydrogen ignites and burns with an almost invisible pale-blue flame. The only product is pure water — clear droplets form on cold surfaces near the reaction. No CO2 is produced. A 'squeaky pop' sound is heard if a small amount of hydrogen is ignited in a test tube. The synthesis of water from its elements is highly exothermic.

reactions.educational_note: Two non-metal gases combine to synthesise liquid water — one of the most fundamental synthesis reactions. This is the reverse of electrolysis of water (decomposition). It proves water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen fuel cells use this exact reaction to generate electricity and water — a clean energy technology.

reactions.name: Nitrogen + Hydrogen → Ammonia (Haber Process)

output.observation: At room temperature and pressure nitrogen and hydrogen do NOT react — nitrogen is very unreactive due to its strong N≡N triple bond. Under industrial conditions (450°C, 200 atm pressure, iron catalyst), the two gases combine to form ammonia (NH3). The product has a sharp, pungent smell. This is the Haber-Bosch process — one of the most important industrial reactions ever discovered.

reactions.educational_note: The Haber process: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. It is a reversible, exothermic synthesis reaction requiring high temperature, high pressure, and an iron catalyst. About 150 million tonnes of ammonia are produced annually, mostly for fertilisers that feed ~half the world's population. A key example of synthesis in industry and the importance of reaction conditions.

reactions.name: Calcium Oxide + Water → Calcium Hydroxide (Slaking of Lime)

output.observation: Water added to calcium oxide causes a dramatic, vigorous reaction — the solid hisses, crackles, swells, and crumbles as steam is released. The beaker becomes very hot. A white suspension of calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is formed. If excess water is added, limewater forms. Temperature rise can be 150–200°C in concentrated reactions.

reactions.educational_note: Metallic oxide + water → metal hydroxide (base). CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2. This is 'slaking of lime' — one of the oldest industrial chemical reactions (used in cement, plaster, and agriculture). The reaction is highly exothermic — CaO was historically used to generate heat in self-heating meal packs. Ca(OH)2 is a weak base used to neutralise acidic soils.

reactions.name: Sulfur Trioxide + Water → Sulfuric Acid

output.observation: Sulfur trioxide dissolves rapidly and violently into water, releasing dense white acid mist. The solution becomes extremely hot as concentrated sulfuric acid forms. The reaction is dangerously exothermic. This is why SO3 from industrial plants contributes to acid rain — it reacts with atmospheric water vapour to produce H2SO4 droplets.

reactions.educational_note: Non-metal oxide + water → acid. SO3 + H2O → H2SO4. This synthesis produces one of the most important industrial chemicals — sulfuric acid. The Contact Process (industrial) makes SO3 first (from burning sulfur), then reacts it with water. SO3 + rainwater → acid rain, causing environmental damage. An important real-world connection for grade 9–10 students.

reactions.name: Sodium + Chlorine → Sodium Chloride (Table Salt)

output.observation: Sodium burns spontaneously and brilliantly in chlorine gas with a bright orange-yellow flame. The yellow-green chlorine colour disappears entirely. White crystalline sodium chloride (common table salt) deposits on the jar walls. The transformation is dramatic — a dangerous reactive metal and a toxic gas combine to make a safe, edible compound.

reactions.educational_note: Metal + non-metal → ionic salt. 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. This is the textbook demonstration of ionic bond formation in synthesis. Sodium transfers its electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that pack into a crystal lattice. The product (salt) is completely safe — the opposite of the hazardous reactants. Shows how properties of compounds differ entirely from their elements.

reactions.name: Aluminium + Chlorine → Aluminium Chloride

output.observation: Aluminium powder ignites readily in chlorine gas with bright white sparks and dense white fumes. The yellow-green chlorine gas is consumed completely. White/pale yellow aluminium chloride solid forms. The reaction is rapid and exothermic. AlCl3 is a covalent chloride (unlike NaCl) and fumes in moist air.

reactions.educational_note: Al + Cl2 → AlCl3. Aluminium chloride is an unusual product — it behaves as a covalent compound despite being metal + non-metal, due to Al's high charge density. AlCl3 is used as a catalyst in organic synthesis (Friedel-Crafts reactions). This contrasts with NaCl synthesis to show how different metals produce different types of chlorides.

reactions.name: Aluminium + Oxygen → Aluminium Oxide

output.observation: Aluminium powder burns with bright white sparks in oxygen to form white aluminium oxide (Al2O3). The reaction is highly exothermic. Al2O3 is an extremely hard, high-melting-point white solid — used in industry as a refractory material. In practice, aluminium objects develop a thin protective Al2O3 layer spontaneously in air, preventing further corrosion.

reactions.educational_note: 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3. Aluminium oxide is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids and bases. It is the basis of corundum (ruby and sapphire gemstones) when trace metals are present. The thermite reaction (Al + Fe2O3) releases enormous heat by using this very synthesis driving force. The natural Al2O3 coating is why aluminium appears unreactive despite being a reactive metal.

reactions.name: Iron + Oxygen → Iron(III) Oxide (Rusting)

output.observation: Iron powder reacts with oxygen slowly at room temperature, forming reddish-brown iron(III) oxide (rust/Fe2O3). The grey iron gradually turns orange-brown. Unlike magnesium or aluminium, iron does not burn in air — it only slowly oxidises. The rust is a non-protective, flaky oxide layer that allows further corrosion below it.

reactions.educational_note: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. Rust is a synthesis reaction but a very slow one — a slow oxidation. Fe2O3 is a basic oxide. Rusting requires both oxygen AND water — removing either prevents rusting (galvanising, painting, oiling). This connects synthesis chemistry to everyday corrosion and materials science. Iron rusting costs economies billions annually in infrastructure damage.

reactions.name: Sodium + Oxygen → Sodium Oxide

output.observation: Sodium burns rapidly in oxygen with a bright characteristic yellow flame, forming white sodium oxide (Na2O). The freshly cut silver sodium surface quickly dulls and turns white. In excess oxygen, sodium peroxide (Na2O2, a yellow solid) can also form. Na2O dissolves vigorously in water to form NaOH (a strong base).

reactions.educational_note: 4Na + O2 → 2Na2O. Sodium oxide is a strongly basic oxide — it reacts vigorously with water (Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH). The bright yellow colour of sodium's flame is due to the sodium emission line at 589 nm — this is the basis of flame tests for sodium ions. In excess O2, Na forms Na2O2 (sodium peroxide), a more complex product than expected.

reactions.name: Hydrogen + Chlorine → Hydrogen Chloride Gas

output.observation: When hydrogen and chlorine are mixed and exposed to light or ignited, they react explosively — the yellow-green chlorine colour disappears completely. Colourless hydrogen chloride gas (HCl) forms with sharp, choking acidic fumes. Moist air turns the HCl into hydrochloric acid droplets, visible as white fumes.

reactions.educational_note: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. This synthesis is triggered by UV light (photochemical synthesis) — a chain reaction via free radicals. HCl gas dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid (strong acid). This reaction shows how two non-metals can synthesise a covalent compound. The H–Cl bond is polar covalent, giving HCl its acidic properties in water.

reactions.name: Magnesium + Chlorine → Magnesium Chloride

output.observation: Magnesium burns vigorously in chlorine gas with a bright white flame. The yellow-green chlorine gas is consumed entirely. White crystalline magnesium chloride (MgCl2) is produced. The reaction is very exothermic. MgCl2 is an ionic salt that dissolves readily in water — used industrially in de-icing roads.

reactions.educational_note: Mg + Cl2 → MgCl2. A reactive metal combining with a halogen gas — a model ionic synthesis. Magnesium loses 2 electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺) while each Cl gains 1 electron (Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻), so 2 Cl⁻ balance one Mg²⁺. This demonstrates how ionic compounds form and why their formulae are determined by charge balance.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Oxygen → Sulfur Dioxide (Step 1 of Contact Process)

output.observation: Sulfur melts then ignites with a distinctive blue flame. The yellow solid completely converts to invisible sulfur dioxide gas (SO2). A sharp, choking smell of SO2 is detected. The gas can be confirmed by testing with damp litmus paper (turns red) or potassium manganate(VII) solution (decolourises). This is Step 1 of the industrial Contact Process to make H2SO4.

reactions.educational_note: S + O2 → SO2. Non-metal + oxygen → acidic oxide. In the industrial Contact Process: Step 1 — S + O2 → SO2; Step 2 — 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3 (V2O5 catalyst); Step 3 — SO3 + H2O → H2SO4. SO2 also forms acid rain when it escapes industrial chimneys: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 (sulfurous acid). Key real-world application of synthesis chemistry.

reactions.name: Nitrogen + Oxygen → Nitrogen Monoxide

output.observation: At room temperature and atmospheric pressure, nitrogen and oxygen do NOT react — both are very stable gases. The reaction only occurs at very high temperatures (above 2000°C), such as in lightning strikes or inside car engine cylinders. The colourless NO gas produced quickly reacts further with oxygen in air to form brown NO2 (nitrogen dioxide).

reactions.educational_note: N2 + O2 → 2NO (only at very high temperatures). This synthesis requires breaking the extremely strong N≡N triple bond (945 kJ/mol). In car engines and during lightning, the high temperatures cause this reaction — producing NOx gases that contribute to smog and acid rain. It demonstrates that not all element combinations react spontaneously — activation energy determines if synthesis occurs.

reactions.name: Magnesium + Sulfur → Magnesium Sulfide

output.observation: When strongly heated, magnesium reacts with sulfur powder with bright flashes. A pale yellowish-white solid, magnesium sulfide (MgS), is formed. MgS is an ionic compound with a characteristic smell when wet (releases H2S on contact with moisture). The reaction is less dramatic than Mg burning in oxygen but follows the same A + B → AB synthesis pattern.

reactions.educational_note: Mg + S → MgS. Magnesium (Group 2, forms Mg²⁺) combines with sulfur (Group 16, forms S²⁻) to form an ionic compound. MgS has the same crystal structure as NaCl. The Mg²⁺:S²⁻ ratio is 1:1 because both ions have the same magnitude charge. This reinforces how ion charges determine compound formulae in ionic synthesis reactions.

reactions.name: Iron + Chlorine → Iron(III) Chloride

output.observation: Iron glows orange-red in chlorine gas. Reddish-brown fumes of iron(III) chloride (FeCl3) are produced and condense as a dark brown-orange crystalline solid on cooler parts of the tube. The yellow-green chlorine gas is consumed. FeCl3 fumes in moist air. This reaction shows chlorine oxidising iron to its +3 oxidation state.

reactions.educational_note: 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3. Iron can form FeCl2 or FeCl3 depending on conditions — with excess chlorine, the higher +3 state (FeCl3) is always produced. FeCl3 is an important industrial catalyst and is used in etching printed circuit boards. This reaction also shows that Cl2 is a strong enough oxidising agent to force iron into a higher oxidation state than typical.

reactions.name: No Reaction — Nitrogen and Water

output.observation: No reaction. Nitrogen gas simply bubbles through water without dissolving significantly or reacting. Nitrogen is extremely unreactive at room temperature due to the very strong N≡N triple bond (945 kJ/mol). The water remains clear and neutral (pH 7). Nitrogen's inertness at room temperature is why it is used to fill food packaging.

reactions.educational_note: Not all elements combine easily — synthesis reactions require enough energy to break existing bonds. The N≡N triple bond is one of the strongest bonds in chemistry, making nitrogen very unreactive at room temperature. This is a key contrast to the Haber Process, where high temperature and pressure are needed to force N2 and H2 to react. Activation energy is essential.

reactions.name: No Direct Reaction — Iron Powder and Water (Slow Rust)
reactions.formula: Fe + H2O -> no immediate synthesis  (slow rusting with O2 present)

output.observation: No immediate synthesis reaction. Iron and water alone do not react rapidly. Rusting is a very slow process that requires BOTH water AND oxygen together. Iron in pure, deoxygenated water does not rust. This is why iron stored underwater in oxygen-free conditions does not corrode — and why rust inhibitors work by blocking oxygen access.

reactions.educational_note: Synthesis does not always occur simply by mixing two substances. Iron rusting (Fe + O2 + H2O → Fe2O3·xH2O) requires both oxygen and water — neither alone is sufficient. This is important for understanding corrosion prevention: remove O2 (vacuum packing), remove H2O (dessicants), or coat the surface (paint, oil, galvanising). Real-world connection to engineering and materials science.

reactions.name: No Reaction — Hydrogen and Water
reactions.formula: H2 + H2O -> no reaction  (at room temperature)

output.observation: Hydrogen gas bubbles through water without any reaction. Hydrogen does not react with water at room temperature. Water is already the product of hydrogen + oxygen synthesis — it cannot react further with hydrogen under normal conditions. The water remains neutral and clear.

reactions.educational_note: H2 and H2O do not react at room temperature. This is a good example of chemical stability — once water is formed, it does not react further with hydrogen. However, at very high temperatures (>2500°C), water can be decomposed back into H2 and O2. This reinforces the concept of reversibility — synthesis reactions can be reversed under extreme conditions.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Chlorine → Disulfur Dichloride

output.observation: Sulfur and chlorine react on gentle heating to form disulfur dichloride (S2Cl2) — an orange-yellow, fuming oily liquid with an intensely unpleasant smell. The yellow-green chlorine gas is absorbed. S2Cl2 fumes strongly in moist air, reacting with water to produce HCl and sulfur. This is a less common but real non-metal + halogen synthesis reaction.

reactions.educational_note: 2S + Cl2 → S2Cl2. Two non-metals combining to form a covalent compound — a synthesis reaction producing a liquid product rather than a solid salt. S2Cl2 is used in rubber vulcanisation. This contrasts with metal + halogen synthesis (which makes ionic solids) and shows that non-metal + halogen synthesis produces covalent molecules with very different physical properties.

reactions.name: No Direct Reaction — Nitrogen and Chlorine at Room Temperature

output.observation: No reaction. Nitrogen and chlorine gases do not react with each other at room temperature. Nitrogen trichloride (NCl3) can be made only through indirect reactions (e.g., ammonia reacting with chlorine), not by direct synthesis. The yellow-green chlorine smell remains as no reaction consumes it.

reactions.educational_note: N2 and Cl2 do not react directly — the N≡N triple bond is too strong to be broken by Cl2 under normal conditions. This shows that not all combinations of elements lead to synthesis reactions. Comparing reactions that work (Na + Cl2, Mg + Cl2, Fe + Cl2) with those that don't (N2 + Cl2) teaches students to evaluate reactivity and bond strength when predicting synthesis outcomes.

reactions.name: Calcium Oxide + Sulfur Trioxide → Calcium Sulfate

output.observation: Calcium oxide absorbs sulfur trioxide gas and reacts to form calcium sulfate (CaSO4, gypsum). The reaction occurs as a white powder absorbs the gas. The SO3 fumes disappear and the white solid product forms. CaSO4 is the familiar 'gypsum' material — used in plaster of Paris, drywall, and cement. This is an acid-base oxide synthesis.

reactions.educational_note: CaO (basic oxide) + SO3 (acidic oxide) → CaSO4 (a salt). This is an oxide-oxide synthesis — an acidic oxide reacting with a basic oxide to form a salt, with no water needed. This pattern (acid oxide + basic oxide → salt) parallels acid + base → salt + water. It explains how flue-gas desulfurisation works in power stations: CaO scrubbers absorb SO3 to prevent acid rain.

reactions.name: No Reaction — Magnesium and Nitrogen at Room Temperature

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Magnesium ribbon does not react with nitrogen gas under normal lab conditions. However, when burning magnesium is placed in nitrogen gas, it does react with a yellow-orange flame to form magnesium nitride (Mg3N2) — a yellow-brown solid. This reaction only proceeds with high activation energy (ignition).

reactions.educational_note: 3Mg + N2 → Mg3N2 only occurs on ignition — not spontaneously. When magnesium burns in air, it actually makes BOTH MgO (reaction with O2) and Mg3N2 (reaction with N2), since air contains 78% N2. This is why the white MgO ash also contains traces of yellow Mg3N2. Mg3N2 reacts with water to release ammonia: Mg3N2 + 6H2O → 3Mg(OH)2 + 2NH3.

reactions.name: Sodium + Water → Sodium Hydroxide + Hydrogen

output.observation: Sodium skitters across the water surface as it reacts vigorously, fizzing rapidly. Hydrogen gas is released — enough to ignite the sodium, burning with a characteristic lilac/violet flame (sodium emission). The water turns alkaline (NaOH forms) — confirmed by universal indicator turning purple. The sodium disappears completely.

reactions.educational_note: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2↑. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is synthesised directly as a product. Note: this is also a displacement reaction (Na displaces H from water). The lilac flame is a flame test for sodium (actually the intense yellow-orange of sodium emission — it appears lilac/violet in the intense reflection). NaOH is a major industrial base used in soap, paper, and textiles.

desk.name: Electrochemistry — Electrolysis & Electrolytes
desk.description: Select any 2 solutions/substances to explore electrochemistry — conductivity tests, electrolysis products at cathode and anode, colour changes, gas evolution, metal deposition, and electroplating.
desk.mode_note: In this desk, one chemical acts as the ELECTROLYTE (solution in the cell) and the second acts as the ELECTRODE MATERIAL or REAGENT. The experiment always uses a DC power supply connected to two electrodes dipped into the electrolyte.

chemicals.name: Silver Nitrate Solution
chemicals.hazard: oxidising — stains skin black; avoid contact

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate — Inert (Graphite) Electrodes

output.color_fade_note: Blue colour fades as Cu2+ ions are removed from solution
output.observation: Pink-brown copper metal deposits on the cathode (negative electrode). Colourless oxygen gas bubbles form at the anode. The blue colour of the solution slowly fades as Cu2+ ions are used up.

reactions.educational_note: Cu2+ ions are reduced at the cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. OH- ions are oxidised at the anode releasing O2. This is reduction at cathode and oxidation at anode — a redox process. The fading blue colour confirms Cu2+ ions are being removed.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate — Active Copper Electrodes (Copper Purification)
reactions.formula: Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-

output.color_change_note: Blue colour stays constant — Cu2+ replenished as fast as it is used
output.observation: Copper deposits on the cathode — it grows heavier. The anode slowly dissolves — it grows lighter. The blue colour of the solution stays constant throughout!

reactions.educational_note: With copper electrodes, the anode dissolves (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-) and copper deposits at cathode (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu). The Cu2+ concentration stays constant — so the blue colour does NOT fade. This principle is used industrially to purify copper.

reactions.name: Copper Sulfate Solution + Zinc Electrode — Displacement (No Electrolysis)

output.observation: Without any electricity — just by placing zinc into copper sulfate — a reddish-brown copper coating appears on the zinc. The blue colour fades. This is a spontaneous displacement, not electrolysis!

reactions.educational_note: Zinc is higher than copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper spontaneously: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu. No electricity needed! The blue colour fades as Cu2+ is removed. This contrasts beautifully with electrolysis — same result, different method.

reactions.name: Copper Sulfate + Silver Nitrate — Two Electrolytes Mixed

output.observation: When mixed, a faint white precipitate of silver sulfate may form. Both are electrolytes, so the mixture still conducts well. No electrolysis reaction occurs without a power supply.

reactions.educational_note: Both CuSO4 and AgNO3 are strong electrolytes. When mixed without power, SO42- and Ag+ can form a slight white precipitate of Ag2SO4. To electrolyse this mixture, a DC power supply would be needed.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Brine (NaCl) — Graphite Electrodes

output.anode_gas_test: bleaches moist litmus paper — turns white
output.observation: Colourless hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) bubbles at the cathode. Yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches litmus) bubbles at the anode. The remaining solution becomes alkaline (NaOH).

reactions.educational_note: The electrolysis of brine is industrially vital — it produces three useful products: H2 (fuel), Cl2 (disinfectant/bleach), and NaOH (used in soap making). At the cathode, H+ ions are discharged in preference to Na+ (Na is too reactive). At the anode, Cl- ions are discharged in preference to OH- when concentration is high.

reactions.name: NaCl Solution + Copper Electrode — Copper Dissolves, No NaCl Electrolysis
reactions.formula: Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- | Cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 (or Na+ stays)

output.anode_product: copper electrode dissolves — Cu2+ ions enter solution
output.color_change_note: Solution gradually turns light blue as Cu2+ ions dissolve from copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen gas bubbles at the cathode with a squeaky pop. The copper anode slowly dissolves, turning the colourless salt solution light blue as Cu2+ ions enter it.

reactions.educational_note: When a copper electrode is used as the anode, it dissolves preferentially — even in NaCl solution. Active anodes are oxidised instead of the solution's anions. The solution turns blue, showing Cu2+ is entering it.

reactions.name: NaCl Solution + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Anode Dissolves

output.observation: Hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) forms at the cathode. The zinc anode slowly corrodes and becomes lighter. The solution remains colourless as Zn2+ is colourless.

reactions.educational_note: Active electrodes (zinc here) dissolve at the anode during electrolysis. Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-. At cathode, H+ from water is reduced to H2 since Na+ is too reactive. This is similar in principle to the zinc-copper galvanic cell.

reactions.name: Brine + Silver Nitrate — AgCl White Precipitate Forms

output.observation: A curdy white precipitate of silver chloride instantly forms when silver nitrate is added to brine. This is the classic halide ion test — confirms chloride ions are present in the solution.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO3. The white precipitate of AgCl is the standard test for Cl- ions (halide test). AgCl is insoluble — even though both reactants dissolved easily. This is not an electrolysis reaction — it is an ionic precipitation.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Dilute H2SO4 — Acidified Water

output.observation: Vigorous bubbling at both electrodes. Hydrogen (2 volumes) at cathode — squeaky pop. Oxygen (1 volume) at anode — relights glowing splint. Volume ratio 2:1 confirms water composition (H2O).

reactions.educational_note: Electrolysis of acidified water decomposes water into H2 and O2. The ratio 2:1 (H2:O2) matches the formula H2O — 2 hydrogens to 1 oxygen. H2SO4 is only a conductor — it is not decomposed. This is how water's composition was first proved experimentally.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Copper Electrode — Copper Anode Dissolves

output.color_change_note: Solution turns blue as Cu2+ ions dissolve from copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen bubbles at the cathode. The copper anode dissolves slowly, turning the colourless acid solution blue as Cu2+ ions are released. The solution gains a noticeable blue tint over time.

reactions.educational_note: Active copper anode dissolves in preference to SO42- or OH- oxidation. Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- at anode; 2H+ + 2e- → H2 at cathode. The solution turning blue is a clear visual indicator of Cu2+ production.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Dissolves, H2 Produced (Without Electricity)
reactions.formula: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (spontaneous acid-metal reaction)

output.observation: No power supply needed! Zinc reacts spontaneously with sulfuric acid — vigorous fizzing with colourless hydrogen gas (squeaky pop). The zinc metal gradually dissolves. This is a metal-acid reaction, NOT electrolysis.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2↑. Zinc reacts with dilute acid without any electricity — it is a simple displacement reaction. This contrasts with electrolysis where an external power supply forces the decomposition. Hydrogen test: burning splint produces a squeaky pop.

reactions.name: H2SO4 + Silver Nitrate — No Precipitate (Both Ionic, Compatible)
reactions.formula: H2SO4 + AgNO3 -> Ag2SO4 (slight white precipitate) + HNO3

output.observation: A faint white precipitate of silver sulfate forms when silver nitrate is added to sulfuric acid. Both solutions are highly conductive electrolytes. No gas produced without a power supply.

reactions.educational_note: H2SO4 + 2AgNO3 → Ag2SO4↓ + 2HNO3. Silver sulfate is sparingly soluble — giving a faint precipitate. This shows that electrolyte solutions can still react chemically even without electricity — through ionic precipitation.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Dilute HCl — H2 at Cathode, Cl2 at Anode

output.anode_gas_test: bleaches moist litmus paper — turns white
output.observation: Hydrogen (squeaky pop) bubbles at the cathode. Pale yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches moist litmus) forms at the anode. Same products as brine but solution is acidic throughout.

reactions.educational_note: HCl fully dissociates: HCl → H+ + Cl-. At cathode: H+ reduced to H2. At anode: Cl- oxidised to Cl2. Unlike NaCl (brine), no NaOH byproduct forms. The chlorine gas test — moist litmus bleached white — is a key school test.

reactions.name: HCl + Copper Electrode — Copper Dissolves, H2 at Cathode

output.color_change_note: Solution turns blue-green as Cu2+ ions enter from dissolving copper anode
output.observation: Hydrogen gas (squeaky pop) at cathode. The copper anode dissolves, and the colourless acid gradually turns blue-green (Cu2+ ions in solution). Two dramatic changes — gas AND colour!

reactions.educational_note: Copper anode dissolves preferentially over Cl- oxidation: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-. Cu2+ in solution gives the characteristic blue-green colour. The H+ at cathode is reduced to H2. This is a visually rich electrolysis experiment.

reactions.name: HCl + Zinc — Spontaneous Reaction (Acid + Metal, No Electricity)

output.observation: Vigorous fizzing immediately — no electricity needed! Zinc dissolves as it reacts with hydrochloric acid. Colourless hydrogen gas with a squeaky pop is produced. This is a straightforward metal + acid reaction.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2↑. Zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from acid spontaneously. No power supply needed. Students should learn to distinguish spontaneous chemical reactions from forced electrolysis.

reactions.name: HCl + Silver Nitrate — White Precipitate of AgCl (Halide Test)

output.precipitate_solubility_test: insoluble in HNO3 — confirms Cl- ion
output.observation: An immediate curdy white precipitate of AgCl forms. This is the classic test for chloride ions. The precipitate is insoluble in dilute nitric acid — this confirms it is AgCl (not AgBr or AgI).

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 + HCl → AgCl↓ + HNO3. AgCl is a curdy white precipitate — insoluble in dilute HNO3. This is the standard school test for Cl- (halide ion test). AgBr gives pale cream; AgI gives yellow. Insolubility in HNO3 confirms chloride.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of NaOH Solution — Water Decomposed to H2 + O2

output.observation: Vigorous gas at both electrodes. Twice as much hydrogen (cathode) as oxygen (anode). Hydrogen: squeaky pop. Oxygen: relights glowing splint. NaOH acts as conductor, not decomposed.

reactions.educational_note: NaOH provides ions (Na+, OH-) making the solution a good conductor, but water is electrolysed — not NaOH. Na+ is too reactive to be discharged at cathode — H2O is reduced instead. The 2:1 ratio of H2:O2 is the key result proving H2O composition.

reactions.name: NaOH Solution + Copper Electrode — Copper Anode Dissolves
reactions.formula: Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e- | Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2 (blue precipitate)

output.anode_product: copper electrode dissolves; Cu(OH)2 blue precipitate forms
output.precipitate_name: Copper Hydroxide Cu(OH)2 — pale blue gelatinous precipitate
output.observation: Hydrogen gas at cathode. Copper anode dissolves releasing Cu2+ ions. These immediately react with OH- in NaOH solution to form pale blue copper hydroxide precipitate. A dramatic double change — gas AND precipitate!

reactions.educational_note: Cu2+ from the dissolving anode reacts with OH- in NaOH: Cu2+ + 2OH- → Cu(OH)2 (blue precipitate). This is a double observation — active electrode behaviour + precipitation. Shows the interaction between electrode material and electrolyte.

reactions.name: NaOH Solution + Zinc Electrode — Zinc Dissolves in Alkali
reactions.formula: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2 (spontaneous — zinc is amphoteric)

output.observation: Zinc slowly dissolves in NaOH solution producing hydrogen gas — even without electricity! This is unusual because zinc reacts with both acids AND alkalis. Gentle bubbling, squeaky pop confirms H2.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Zn + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2↑ (sodium zincate). This spontaneous reaction demonstrates amphoteric behaviour — an important Grade 10 concept.

reactions.name: NaOH + Silver Nitrate — Brown/Black Silver Oxide Precipitate

output.observation: A dark brown/black precipitate of silver oxide instantly forms. The mixture turns muddy brown. Silver nitrate + alkali is a dramatic reaction — the precipitate is very dark and insoluble.

reactions.educational_note: 2AgNO3 + 2NaOH → Ag2O↓ + 2NaNO3 + H2O. Silver oxide is the dark brown/black precipitate. This reaction is used in qualitative analysis to confirm Ag+ ions. Contrasts with AgCl (white) from Cl- test.

reactions.name: Glucose Solution — Non-Electrolyte, No Conduction

output.observation: The bulb does NOT light up. No bubbles at either electrode. Glucose dissolves in water but does NOT form ions — it is a non-electrolyte and cannot conduct electricity.

reactions.educational_note: Glucose (C6H12O6) is a molecular (covalent) compound. It dissolves in water but does NOT dissociate into ions. No ions = no current = no electrolysis. This is the key difference between electrolytes (ionic) and non-electrolytes (molecular).

reactions.name: Glucose Solution + Copper Electrode — No Reaction
reactions.formula: C6H12O6 (aq) + Cu — no conduction, no electrolysis

output.observation: The bulb stays off. No reaction at copper electrodes. Glucose is a non-electrolyte — no ions means no current, no electrolysis, and no electrode reactions.

reactions.educational_note: Even with a reactive metal electrode, if the solution is a non-electrolyte, no current can flow and no electrolysis occurs. Both an ionic electrolyte AND a complete circuit are required.

reactions.name: Glucose Solution + Zinc — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction at all. Zinc does not react with glucose solution (unlike with acids or alkalis). No gas, no colour change, no current flow — glucose is a non-electrolyte.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc reacts with acids (H+) and alkalis (OH-) but not with neutral non-electrolytes like glucose. No ions means no driving force for a chemical or electrochemical reaction.

reactions.name: Glucose + Silver Nitrate — Tollens'-like Silver Mirror Reaction
reactions.formula: C6H12O6 + 2Ag+ -> C6H12O7 + 2Ag (silver mirror — with ammonia and heat)

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — shiny mirror on glass wall
output.observation: When heated gently with silver nitrate (and ammonia), glucose acts as a reducing agent — silver ions are reduced to shiny silver metal forming a mirror on the glass wall. This shows glucose is a reducing sugar.

reactions.educational_note: Glucose is a reducing sugar — it donates electrons to Ag+ reducing it to Ag metal (the silver mirror test / Tollens' test). This shows glucose can participate in redox reactions even though it is a non-electrolyte. It does NOT conduct electricity, but it CAN reduce metal ions chemically.

reactions.name: Distilled Water — Very Poor Conductor, Almost No Electrolysis

output.observation: The bulb does NOT light up — or shows only the faintest glow. No visible gas at electrodes. Pure water is an extremely poor conductor because it has almost no free ions.

reactions.educational_note: Pure water has an extremely low ion concentration (Kw = 10-14). It is effectively a non-conductor. This is why tap water conducts (dissolved minerals) but distilled water does not. Adding an electrolyte like H2SO4 dramatically increases conductivity.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Copper Electrode — No Electrolysis
reactions.formula: H2O + Cu electrode — negligible current, no useful electrolysis

output.observation: No visible reaction. Distilled water has no ions, so even copper electrodes cannot drive any useful electrolysis. The bulb stays off completely.

reactions.educational_note: Even a reactive active electrode cannot compensate for the absence of charge carriers (ions). Distilled water + copper electrodes = no circuit completion, no electrolysis.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Zinc — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Zn + H2O -> no reaction at room temperature

output.observation: No reaction. Zinc does not react with distilled water at room temperature. No bubbles, no colour change. Zinc only reacts with steam at high temperatures.

reactions.educational_note: Zinc + water → no reaction at room temperature (unlike very reactive metals such as sodium or potassium). Zinc needs steam (very high temperature) or an acid/alkali to react. This is a useful reminder of the reactivity series.

reactions.name: Distilled Water + Silver Nitrate — AgNO3 Dissolves Easily

output.observation: Silver nitrate dissolves completely and instantly in distilled water to give a clear, colourless solution. The solution now conducts electricity — the bulb lights up. AgNO3 is a strong electrolyte.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 is an ionic compound — it fully dissociates: AgNO3 → Ag+ + NO3-. These free ions carry the current. This experiment beautifully contrasts distilled water (no conduction) with AgNO3 solution (bright bulb) — showing that ions are essential for conductivity.

reactions.name: Electrolysis of Copper Chloride — Cu Deposit + Cl2 Gas

output.color_fade_note: Blue-green colour fades as Cu2+ and Cl- ions are removed
output.observation: Pink-brown copper deposits on the cathode. Pale yellow-green chlorine gas (bleaches moist litmus) bubbles at the anode. The blue-green solution gradually fades as BOTH Cu2+ and Cl- ions are removed.

reactions.educational_note: CuCl2 → Cu2+ + 2Cl-. At cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (pink deposit). At anode: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (yellow-green gas bleaches litmus). The solution fades as BOTH ions are removed — unlike CuSO4 where only Cu2+ is removed.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Copper Electrodes — Copper Transfer (Electroplating)
reactions.formula: Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | Anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-

output.color_change_note: Colour stays constant — Cu2+ consumed and replenished equally
output.observation: Copper deposits on cathode; copper anode slowly dissolves. The blue-green colour stays constant — confirming Cu2+ is continuously replenished. This is the electroplating principle: coating objects with copper.

reactions.educational_note: With active copper electrodes in CuCl2: the cathode gains copper; the anode loses copper. [Cu2+] stays constant. This is the basis of electroplating — useful for coating jewellery, circuit boards, and industrial parts with a layer of copper.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Zinc Electrode — Displacement Without Electricity

output.observation: No electricity needed! Zinc placed into copper chloride solution immediately gets coated in reddish-brown copper. The blue-green colour fades. Zinc is more reactive than copper — it spontaneously displaces it.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + CuCl2 → ZnCl2 + Cu. Zinc displaces copper spontaneously — no power supply needed. The reactivity series predicts this: Zn > Cu. This is a galvanic (spontaneous) reaction, contrasted with forced electrolysis.

reactions.name: CuCl2 + Silver Nitrate — White AgCl AND Blue Cu2+ Persist

output.precipitate_name: Silver Chloride (AgCl) — curdy white precipitate in blue-green solution
output.observation: A white precipitate of AgCl forms instantly. But the solution remains blue-green — because Cu2+ ions do NOT precipitate with NO3-. You can see white flakes in a blue-green liquid — a striking contrast.

reactions.educational_note: AgNO3 precipitates Cl- as AgCl (white). But Cu(NO3)2 stays in solution — blue-green. This elegant result shows selective precipitation: Cl- is removed but Cu2+ stays. Confirms Cl- presence (halide test) even in a blue-green electrolyte.

reactions.name: Graphite Electrode + Copper Electrode — Galvanic Cell Setup
reactions.formula: Graphite (cathode) + Cu (anode) in electrolyte -> small voltage generated

output.bulb_brightness: none — needs electrolyte to complete circuit
output.observation: Two solid electrodes placed together without a solution produce no reaction and no voltage. An electrolyte solution is needed to complete the circuit. This setup alone is incomplete.

reactions.educational_note: Electrodes alone do nothing — a complete electrochemical circuit requires: two electrodes + an electrolyte solution + connecting wires + a DC source (for electrolysis) OR a spontaneous redox driving force (for galvanic cells). No electrolyte = open circuit.

reactions.name: Graphite + Zinc — Zinc-Carbon Galvanic Cell (Dry Cell Concept)
reactions.formula: Anode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- | Cathode: (reduction at graphite) — needs electrolyte

output.observation: Graphite and zinc electrodes alone do nothing. But this is the exact same combination as an everyday dry cell (AA battery)! In a battery, the electrolyte (ammonium chloride paste) connects them. Without it — no current.

reactions.educational_note: A zinc-carbon dry cell (AA battery) uses graphite (positive/cathode) and zinc (negative/anode) with ammonium chloride paste as electrolyte. Without the electrolyte, no circuit is complete and no current flows. This pair shows the importance of the electrolyte in any cell.

reactions.name: Graphite Electrode + Silver Nitrate — Electroplating with Silver
reactions.formula: Cathode (graphite): Ag+ + e- -> Ag | Anode: needs silver or inert anode

output.cathode_product: shiny silver metal deposits on graphite cathode
output.anode_product: O2 gas if inert anode used
output.observation: With DC power, shiny silver metal deposits on the graphite cathode — it turns silvery! Ag+ ions from the silver nitrate solution are reduced to Ag metal. This is the principle of silver electroplating.

reactions.educational_note: Silver electroplating: Ag+ + e- → Ag at cathode. The graphite acts as the object to be plated. Industrially, jewellery and cutlery are silver-plated this way using AgNO3 as electrolyte and a silver anode. This demonstrates a real-world electrochemistry application.

reactions.name: Copper + Zinc Electrodes — Galvanic Cell (Simple Battery)
reactions.formula: Anode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- | Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu | EMF ~1.1V

output.observation: When connected in an electrolyte, the voltmeter deflects — a voltage is produced! Zinc is the negative terminal (anode); copper is the positive terminal (cathode). This is a simple galvanic cell — a battery! No power supply needed.

reactions.educational_note: Zn-Cu in electrolyte = a galvanic (voltaic) cell. Zn loses electrons (oxidised at anode); Cu2+ gains electrons (reduced at cathode). EMF ≈ 1.1V. This is the Daniell cell — the first practical battery. Shows spontaneous redox reactions produce electricity.

reactions.name: Copper + Silver Nitrate — Copper Displaces Silver (No Electricity)

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — feathery/spiky silver crystals on copper surface
output.observation: No electricity needed! Feathery silver crystals grow on the copper surface. The colourless solution slowly turns blue as Cu2+ ions enter. Copper is displacing silver — stunning to observe!

reactions.educational_note: Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag. Copper is above silver in the reactivity series — it displaces silver spontaneously. The beautiful dendritic silver crystals and the blue Cu2+ colour change make this a visually dramatic experiment. No electricity needed — it is a galvanic/spontaneous redox reaction.

reactions.name: Zinc + Silver Nitrate — Zinc Displaces Silver

output.precipitate_name: Silver metal — grey metallic precipitate on zinc
output.observation: Silver metal deposits on the zinc surface — no electricity needed! Zinc is higher than silver in the reactivity series, so it displaces silver rapidly. Grey metallic sheen appears on the zinc. Faster than Cu + AgNO3.

reactions.educational_note: Zn + 2AgNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag. Zinc is more reactive than silver — displaces it spontaneously. No power needed. Zn(NO3)2 is colourless, so no colour change in the solution (unlike Cu + AgNO3 which turns blue). Reactivity series: Zn > Cu > Ag.
